demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
issues.explanation: For a 68-year-old retired patient, 'Overworking' is questionable as phrased because it implies a current work role; while keeping busy with tasks is plausible, the specific work-focused item is a poor fit to the demographic context.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is hard to link coherently to the indexed trauma of unexpected death of a loved one and to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance concerns that are not reflected in the threat or appraisal items and does not fit the formulation's main Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat loop.

issues.item: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: For trauma type of unexpected death of a loved one, 'Avoid Being Touched' is hard to explain clinically unless there is interpersonal assault or bodily violation content, which is not present elsewhere in the profile. It appears mismatched to the trauma context and to the other selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' suggests shame about appearance/performance or social evaluative threat, but the rest of the profile centers bereavement-related guilt, isolation, and generalized danger. This strategy does not connect well to the stated trauma type or to the active appraisal-threat loop.

issues.item: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
issues.explanation: The threat items depict pervasive physical danger and inability to feel safe anywhere. In bereavement PTSD this can occur, but here the appraisals provided are mainly isolation and self-blame rather than danger-based meanings. The strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat loop is not well reflected because the appraisals do not explain this specific form of persistent external danger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and the trauma type of traumatic bereavement. The other selected items center on grief-related self-blame, isolation, and generalized danger, but fear of being evaluated for appearance/performance suggests a social-evaluative concern not otherwise represented in threat, memory, triggers, or appraisals.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: 'Self-Blame' can occur after the unexpected death of a loved one, but in this profile it sits awkwardly beside the chosen maladaptive strategies and threat items. If the patient blames herself for the death, one would expect linked strategies or threat content tied to guilt, responsibility, rumination, or death-related cues; instead the profile emphasizes social withdrawal and generic unsafety, making this item insufficiently integrated with the rest.

issues.item: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
issues.explanation: 'Cannot Trust Safety' is not impossible in PTSD, but with traumatic bereavement and no trigger or memory items selected, the threat profile becomes very generalized. In combination with the social-evaluative avoidance item, it creates a mixed formulation in which the source of danger is unclear: bereavement-related guilt/loss versus broad physical danger versus fear of scrutiny. This weakens coherence across nodes given the active Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat linkage.

vignette:
Marguerite Calloway is a 68-year-old retired schoolteacher who presented for her initial intake following the sudden death of her adult son, Daniel, fourteen months ago. Daniel, who was 44 at the time, collapsed at a family barbecue in the backyard of the home he had shared with Marguerite and her husband, Gerald, for the past two years while he managed a difficult divorce. He was gone before the ambulance arrived. Marguerite had been the first to reach him, kneeling on the grass beside the picnic table where he had been laughing only moments before, calling his name while the other guests stood frozen. The cardiac event was entirely without warning. There had been no prior diagnosis, no visible distress, nothing she could have read or acted on - and yet she had come to believe, with a certainty that felt immovable, that she had failed him. She had been a mother. She should have known something was wrong. She should have insisted he see a cardiologist after the mild chest complaint he had mentioned in passing the previous winter. That she had not was, in her mind, an unforgivable lapse.

In the weeks following Daniel's death, Marguerite's body seemed to have registered a threat that her conscious mind could not fully articulate. She described a persistent physical tension - a tautness across her shoulders and jaw, a readiness in her limbs - that did not ease even when she was sitting quietly in her own living room. She had not been able to relax in the way she once could, not during television programmes she used to enjoy, not during the long evenings with Gerald, not even during sleep. Her body appeared to have settled into a state of vigilance that no amount of stillness could interrupt, and strong surges of emotion - fear, horror, guilt, and something she named as shame - arose unpredictably and with a force that frightened her.

What she had done with all of this, steadily and with considerable discipline, was keep moving. She filled her days with tasks: reorganising cupboards, volunteering at the local library two mornings a week, tending to a garden that had never been so meticulously kept. Busyness had become the architecture of her survival. But alongside this relentless activity, she had quietly withdrawn from the social world she and Gerald had occupied together for decades. The neighbours who had attended that barbecue, the couples from their church group, the women she had met with monthly for a book club - she had stopped seeing all of them. The thought of sitting across from someone who had been in that backyard, who had witnessed what happened, who might look at her with pity or, worse, with the same silent question she asked herself, was something she could not face. Over the months, invitations had tapered off, as they do when they are consistently declined, and Marguerite had not tried to reverse this. Gerald attended church alone now. He had stopped asking her to come.

What frightened her most was not the grief itself but what the withdrawal had confirmed to her about her place in the world. She had come to feel that she no longer belonged anywhere - not among the friends who had known her as Daniel's mother and a woman of warmth and competence, not among other bereaved parents whose losses felt different from hers, not even fully within her marriage, where Gerald's quiet steadiness seemed to belong to a version of life she could no longer access. She felt set apart, as though the afternoon in the backyard had moved her permanently to a different side of something, and the people on the other side could not see it.

It was Gerald who finally persuaded her to seek help, after she declined to attend their granddaughter's birthday party - an event she had previously circled on the calendar with delight. Sitting in the intake session, Marguerite was composed and precise, a woman long accustomed to managing herself in front of others. What she said she most hoped for was to stop feeling as though she no longer had a place among the living. What she most feared was that she was right.
